Crash Course Philosophy is brought to you
by Squarespace. Squarespace: share your passion with the world. What gives your life meaning?
God? Love? Money? Work? Fanfiction? Football? Shopping? Sherlock? You might have your own personal sense of
purpose in your life, or maybe you’re hoping this course will
help you find one. Or you might believe that you were created with a certain essence as a human being, with a purpose given to you by God. Whatever the case is, no one would fault you
for wanting your life to have meaning. A sense of meaning is something that we all
crave – maybe even need. And as we move out of our unit on the philosophy
of religion, we should spend some time talking about how
we understand our lives as being meaningful. Because when you think about it, a lot of us devote a ton of energy to the task of finding meaning in our lives. Maybe you find it through religion, or by
fighting for social justice, or educating others, or seeking beauty in artistic expression. No matter how you do it, there’s a group
of philosophers, the existentialists, who say that any, or all, of these things
can give your life meaning. But at the same time, they say: None of them
can. [Theme Music] As you know by now, philosophy is about the dialectic: Someone puts forth an idea, and then someone else responds to it. Sometimes, the response comes right away.
In other cases, it takes thousands of years. Way back in ancient Greece, Plato and Aristotle
took it as given that everything has an essence – a certain set of core properties that are necessary,
or essential – for a thing to be what it is. If those properties were missing, then that
thing would be a different thing. For instance, a knife could have a wooden
handle or a metal handle – it really doesn’t matter. But if it didn’t have a blade, it wouldn’t
really be a knife anymore. The blade is the essential property of the knife, because it gives the knife its defining function. Now, Plato and Aristotle thought that everything
has an essence – including us. And they believed that our essences exist
in us before we’re even born. So by this thinking, part of what it means
to be a good human is to adhere to your essence. Now, you may or may not know what your essence
is, and you might be great at living up to your
essence, or you may be awful at it. But the important thing is that your essence
gives you a purpose. Because you were born to be a certain thing. This belief, known as essentialism, was the standard view of the universe all the way up until the late 19th century, and it’s still accepted by many people today. But in the late 1800s, some thinkers started to challenge the idea that we are imbued with any essence or purpose. German philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche, for
example, embraced nihilism, the belief in the ultimate
meaningless of life. But by the mid-20th century, the path had
been paved for French thinker Jean-Paul Sartre to return
to the question of essence and ask: What if we exist first? What if we’re born without any hard-wired purpose? And then it’s up to us to find our own essences? Well this became the framework for what we
now know as existentialism. And its mantra is the claim that “existence
precedes essence.” In other words, our existence – our birth
– happens first. Then, it’s up to each of us to determine
who we are. We have to write our own essence, through
the way we choose to live. But we have no actual, predetermined purpose
– there’s no set path that we’re supposed to follow. It’s hard to express how radical this idea
was at the time. Because, for thousands of years, you didn’t
have to choose a path, or find your purpose. God did it for you. But it’s important to note that existentialism
is not synonymous with atheism. Plenty of existentialists are atheists, but
some are theists, like Kierkegaard. What theistic existentialists deny is any
sort of teleology – that is, they refute the notion that God made the universe, or our world, or us, with any particular purpose in mind. So, God may exist – but instilling you,
or your life, or the cosmos, with meaning – that’s just not in his job description. As a result, we are each born into a universe
in which we, and our world, and our actions, lack any real,
inherent importance. This is a fundamental component of existentialism. And its adherents refer to it as “the absurd.” You and I think of absurdity as something
that’s just silly, or preposterous. But for existentialists, absurdity is a technical
term. It’s how they describe the search for answers
in an answerless world. We are creatures who need meaning, but we’re
abandoned in a universe full of meaninglessness. So we cry into the wilderness, and get no
response. But we keep crying anyway. That, for an existentialist, is the definition
of absurd. Since there’s no teleology, the world wasn’t created for a reason, and it doesn’t exist for a reason. And if there’s no reason for any of this,
then there’s also no absolutes to abide by: There’s no cosmic justice, no fairness,
no order, no rules. Now, existentialism has its roots in late-19th-century
thinkers like Kierkegaard and Nietzsche. But it really came into its own during and
after World War II, as the horrors of the Holocaust led many people
to abandon any belief in an ordered world. And who could blame them? When Nazis became possible, meaning became
much harder to find. But Sartre faced meaninglessness head-on, and explored one of the most agonizing aspects of existentialism. Not the world’s lack of meaning.
But its terrifying abundance of freedom. To most of us, freedom sounds pretty great. But Sartre thought that we are painfully, shockingly free. After all, if there are no guidelines for
our actions, then each of us is forced to design our own
moral code, to invent a morality to live by.

### Crash Course Philosophy Summary

This transcript reviews the concepts of meaning and purpose in life through the lens of philosophy. 

**Origins of Philosophical Inquiry**

The video discusses the core concept that each individual seeks purpose in their lives - a quest for what gives meaning to existence. This notion draws from the ideas of early philosophers who posited that everything has an essential nature, defining its functions and essence. 

  - Plato and Aristotle believed that these fundamental qualities predestined individuals' roles in the world - the "knife" example serves as illustrative evidence for this idea.
  - Their philosophies persisted significantly during history before evolving into existentialism – meaning the focus shifted towards human existence and how we shape our own life purpose. 

**Existentialism Explained**

The video highlights a paradigm shift in philosophy thanks to key thinkers:

   * **Jean-Paul Sartre**: challenged traditional existential ideas about predetermined purpose, emphasizing that "existence precedes essence." This suggests one's free will shapes their identity and purpose, as opposed to pre-determined roles or expectations.

  * **Nietzsche**: explored the concept of nihilism, suggesting a lack of inherent meaning in life, leading him to endorse non-teleological (random) beliefs about existence and purpose. 

**The Absurdity of Existence**
 The video delves into the heart of existentialist theories: "absurd." It's defined as the search for answers on the existence of meaning while being confronted with a universe inherently lacking purpose, leading to a sense of loneliness and despair in a world devoid of inherent meaning.

 **The Impact of World Wars**
The discussion explores how the backdrop of major societal events like World War II, particularly the Holocaust, significantly impacted individuals' understanding about the human condition on planet Earth.

**Freedom and Responsibility**
Sartre's central concept highlights freedom – with the absence of inherent direction or moral guidelines creates an immense pressure to craft one's unique ethical framework for action. He suggests that this lack of objective moral structures poses a substantial struggle in navigating life.

### The Dialectic of Philosophy 

**Essentialism and Existentialism**

Philosophy revolves around a dialectical process, where one idea challenges another.  Ancient Greeks like Plato and Aristotle established the concept that everything possesses an inherent essence – a defining set of properties essential to its identity (e.g., a knife requires a blade for its function). These essences, they believed, existed in humans as well and guided their lives, making "being a good person" about adhering to one's true self.  This view dominated philosophy until the late 19th century when thinkers challenged it, emphasizing existence before essence.

**The Rejection of Predetermined Purpose: The Rise of Existentialism**

After Nietzsche embraced nihilism and questioned the inherent purpose in life, Jean-Paul Sartre introduced existentialism emphasizing that meaning is derived from action through our experiences.  Sartre’s claim: “existence precedes essence,” suggesting humans first exist before defining their essences through experiences shaping them. This radical idea challenged pre-determined purposes and societal expectations. 

**Existence Precedes Essence – The Absurdity of Existence**

Existentialism arose in response to the horrors of World War II where life lacked meaning, contributing the absurdity that comes with our freedom of choice in a meaningless world.  It led many people to question established authority and seek authenticity. They questioned authority figures like governments, religious institutions, and parents as they were all human subjects without ultimate answers. The concept of bad faith – essentially rejecting existence's meaninglessness by pursuing external guidance – became a defining aspect of existentialism.

**Key Figures and Their Concepts:**

* **Kierkegaard:** Laid the foundation for existentialism with his complex explorations of angst, despair, and religious freedom.

* **Nietzsche:** Embraced nihilism, challenging traditional notions of meaning, purpose, and value in life.
* **Sartre:** Proposed "being condemned to be free" as a consequence for humans lacking inherent meaning.
 
**Beyond Traditional Norms and Ideas:** Existentialism's core concern lies with exploring these existential questions in a world defined by absurdity -  meaninglessness and freedom at the same time.

### The Essence of Existence: Understanding Existentialism

**Essentialism and its Discontent:** 
For centuries, people believed they had a predetermined essence or purpose in life. However, from the late 19th century, philosophers began questioning this notion.  The concept of "essentialism" faded as thinkers like Friedrich Nietzsche embraced nihilism, believing that life inherently lacked meaning, while Jean-Paul Sartre developed existentialism, asserting that we create our own meanings.

**Existentialism and its tenets:**
This philosophical shift challenged the notion of inherent purpose, proposing instead that existence precedes essence (in short, existence is what defines us), a radical idea at the time. This concept was encapsulated in the expression "existence precedes essence."  It suggests human beings create their own identity and direction through their actions within the absence of predetermined meaning. This emphasis on individual freedom is the essence of existentialism: the responsibility to create one's purpose, free from any guiding forces of divinity or pre-determined paths.

**The Absurdity of Existence:**
Existentialists viewed existence without inherent meaning as "absurd," a state of searching for answers in a world devoid of them. This can leave us feeling lost and meaningless. Despite this lack of inherent order, the pursuit of purpose and authenticity is vital.  


**Sartre's Confronting Freedom.** 
This philosophical system was deeply influenced by World War II's upheavals. The atrocities of the Holocaust led many individuals to search for meaning within a world perceived as devoid of it.  Jean-Paul Sartre confronted this existential void head-on through his exploration of "condemnation to be free.”  Sartre thought freedom, even in its terrifying magnitude, necessitates the absence of authority or guides—a stark truth that he believed forced individuals to create their own moral code, essentially invent a sense of "morality" as they choose. In this way, Sartre challenged traditional notions of morals and duty, proposing instead individual autonomy and authentic self-discovery as core concepts for decision making.

**Living Authentically:** 
Sartre viewed "authentic living" as embracing freedom's weight; recognizing that without the weight of choosing our own path, our lives become filled with emptiness or an empty facade of something else's will.


**An Example Through Sartre's Young Man:**  
To illustrate these concepts more clearly, Sartre used a student's dilemma: he was torn between serving a cause while leaving his ailing mother behind or staying and caring for her. This internal decision highlighted the existential principle - individual choice; in this case the act of making the best possible decision despite potential consequences with an understanding that one cannot seek an answer to the decision from others.  



In essence, existentialism argues: freedom, responsibility, and self-creation are the hallmarks of human existence. Our meaning comes not from external forces but by embracing this autonomy within the reality of life's absurdity but also its inherent possibility to have our part in shaping a meaningful experience within that life itself.

### Existentialism: Meaning is In Pursuit

**Origins and Core Principles:**  Existentialism rose from the ashes of World War II, a period marked by profound questioning of societal structures. This philosophical movement stemmed from thinkers like Kierkegaard and Nietzsche and focused on the individual's existence before any predetermined meaning.

**Rejecting Teleology:** Existentialists reject the notion that divine purpose pre-determined the existence of humans or their world. There is no set goal, no inherent meaning in creation. Therefore, the human search for meaning is inherently paradoxical, as they are faced with a meaningless universe, thus questioning "Why?". 

**Understanding "The Absurd"**: The term "absurd" signifies humanity's confrontation with this lack of inherent purpose and its consequences.  Existentialists see this quest for truth in a world lacking defined boundaries, leading to an awareness that they hold agency for meaning creation.  

**Sartre's Philosophy and Freedom** The prominent existentialist Jean-Paul Sartre believed individuals face "condemnation to be free", burdened by freedom within a meaningless universe. This meant responsibility for one's own moral code. He argued against relying on external frameworks; one must choose what forms their personal values and build a meaning system around them.  He referred to this as “bad faith” - the act of avoiding acknowledging, "the absurd," or trying to find meaning through external forces. 

- **Authenticity:** For Sartre, choosing authentically—conforming to one's own chosen value system—was paramount for living a meaningful life despite the absurdity of existence. 

**Example:  The Young Man and Choice:** In a classic example of human choice within the existentialist framework, Sartre describes a predicament where an individual face several choices. There are two paths open before him: Join the military to pursue his own values in accordance with a cause he believed in; or stick around and prioritize his responsibility towards his mother instead of war. This dilemma reveals how individuals must find meaning from their decision to make meaning to life itself. 


**Meaningful Lives:** Existentialists believe personal creation of meaning is vital for a fulfilling existence, even outside the traditional confines of society or religion. Even in seemingly empty environments, meaning can still be given.  
 **The World Without Purpose (and Meaning):** Most of us find a sense of purpose by creating some kind of order and meaning in our lives. For many, this creates a form of stability and satisfaction which allows them to live more fulfilling lives. 


By assigning meaning through their choices—not by passively waiting for external determinants to shape existence. Ultimately, individuals have a responsibility and are empowered to forge their own paths and make the choice that resonates with them, shaping their understanding of life’s “why.”
